title: The Blood of Abel and the Value of One Human Life
subtitle: Genesis 4:8–10 · Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 · Qur'an 5:32
summary: A source-anchored comparison of the murder of Abel, the rabbinic warning to capital witnesses that destroying one soul destroys an entire world, and the Quranic decree to the Children of Israel that slaying one innocent soul is like slaying all mankind.

contextGuard.misuseNotice: Both Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Qur'an 5:32 must be read in their complete judicial and historical contexts. In the Mishnah, this is an admonition to witnesses in capital murder trials; in the Qur'an, it is explicitly introduced as a divine decree previously given to the Children of Israel.

slots.label: The Plural Bloods of the Slain Brother
slots.description: How the biblical text uses the plural 'bloods' (damim) to imply all future generations.

genesis-4.summary: God asks Cain where Abel is; when Cain deflects ('Am I my brother's keeper?'), God declares that the voice of his brother's bloods (*dəmê*, plural) cries out from the ground.
genesis-4.verbatimExcerpt: Yahweh said to Cain, 'Where is Abel, your brother?' He said, 'I don't know. Am I my brother's keeper?' Yahweh said, 'What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.'
genesis-4.limits: In Hebrew, 'blood' in Genesis 4:10 is in the plural (*kol dəmê aḥîḵā*), which forms the linguistic anchor for subsequent rabbinic midrash.

mishnah-sanhedrin.summary: The court admonishes witnesses that in capital cases, the blood of the accused and the blood of all his potential descendants until the end of the world is hanging upon them, citing the plural 'bloods' in Genesis 4:10.
mishnah-sanhedrin.verbatimExcerpt: In capital cases the witness is held responsible for the blood of the accused and the blood of his descendants until the end of the world. For so we find with Cain, who killed his brother, as it is written: 'The voice of the bloods of your brother cries out to Me from the ground' (Genesis 4:10). It does not say 'the blood of your brother', but rather 'the bloods of your brother'—his blood and the blood of his descendants.
mishnah-sanhedrin.limits: Applied specifically as a courtroom warning against false testimony in capital proceedings.

quran-5-32.summary: The Qur'an recounts the story of Adam's two sons (Cain and Abel / Qabil and Habil), where one offers an acceptable sacrifice and the other murders him in envy, followed by a raven showing him how to hide the corpse.
quran-5-32.verbatimExcerpt: And recite unto them the story of the two sons of Adam with truth, when they offered each a sacrifice, and it was accepted from the one of them and was not accepted from the other... But the (other's) mind facilitated to him the murder of his brother, so he murdered him and became one of the losers. Then Allah sent a raven scratching up the ground, to show him how to hide his brother's naked corpse.
quran-5-32.limits: Directly precedes the overarching moral decree of verse 5:32.

slots.label: The Moral Maxim: Slaying One Life vs. Slaying All
slots.description: The formulation equating the preservation or destruction of a single human being to that of the entire world.

genesis-4.summary: Genesis records the universal cosmic weight of murder: the earth itself opens its mouth to receive brotherly blood, bringing wandering and estrangement.
genesis-4.verbatimExcerpt: Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. From now on, when you till the ground, it won't yield its strength to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth.
genesis-4.limits: The explicit formulation ('he who destroys one life...') is not in Genesis; it is the later rabbinic and Quranic deduction from the Cain narrative.

mishnah-sanhedrin.summary: Man was created singular to teach that whoever destroys a single life, scripture considers it as if they destroyed a whole world; and whoever saves a single life, it is as if they saved a whole world.
mishnah-sanhedrin.verbatimExcerpt: Therefore, humanity was created single, to teach you that whoever destroys a single soul, Scripture accounts it to him as if he had destroyed a whole world; and whoever saves a single soul, Scripture accounts it to him as if he had saved a whole world.
mishnah-sanhedrin.limits: Manuscripts differ between 'a single soul' (*nefesh ahat*, e.g. Kaufmann MS) and 'a single soul of Israel' (*nefesh ahat mi-yisrael*, in some printed editions).

quran-5-32.summary: For that cause, Allah decreed unto the Children of Israel that whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.
quran-5-32.verbatimExcerpt: For that cause We decreed for the Children of Israel that whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as that he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as that he had saved the life of all mankind. Our messengers came unto them of old with clear proofs, yet afterwards lo! many of them became prodigals in the earth.
quran-5-32.limits: The Qur'an explicitly states that this was a legal decree given to the Children of Israel (*katabna 'ala bani isra'il*), reflecting the Mishnaic halakhah.

slots.label: The Uniqueness of Each Soul & Judicial Gravity
slots.description: Why mankind was created from a single progenitor: divine coin minting and the cosmic consequence of individual judgment.

genesis-4.summary: Cain cries that his punishment is greater than he can bear; Yahweh appoints a mark for Cain lest anyone finding him should strike him, declaring sevenfold vengeance upon any slayer.
genesis-4.verbatimExcerpt: Cain said to Yahweh, 'My punishment is greater than I can bear... whoever finds me will kill me.' Yahweh said to him, 'Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.' Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, lest any finding him should strike him.
genesis-4.limits: Demonstrates divine restraint on vigilante blood feuds following the first murder.

mishnah-sanhedrin.summary: To proclaim God's greatness: when a human mints coins from one mold, they are all identical, but the Holy One fashioned all humans from the seal of Adam, yet not one is identical to another.
mishnah-sanhedrin.verbatimExcerpt: And to proclaim the greatness of the Holy One, blessed be He: for if a person strikes many coins from one mold, they all resemble one another; but the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, fashioned every person in the stamp of the first man, and yet not one of them resembles his fellow. Therefore every single person is obligated to say: 'For my sake the world was created.'
mishnah-sanhedrin.limits: Emphasizes the infinite and irreplaceable value of every single unique human being.

quran-5-32.summary: The Qur'an details the strict judicial boundaries and penalties for violent rebellion or corruption in the land (*fasad fi al-ard*), while offering pardon for those who repent before apprehension.
quran-5-32.verbatimExcerpt: The only reward of those who make war upon Allah and His messenger and strive after corruption in the land will be that they will be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet on alternate sides cut off, or will be expelled out of the land... Save those who repent before ye overpower them. For know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
quran-5-32.limits: Establishes legal penalties strictly for active violent corruption and highway robbery (*hirabah*), forbidding arbitrary bloodshed.

edges.basisNote: Scholarly consensus identifies Qur'an 5:32 as a direct and conscious intertextual citation of the Rabbinic Mishnaic formulation in Sanhedrin 4:5. The Qur'an itself introduces the teaching by explicitly attributing it as a past divine decree given to the Children of Israel ('For that cause We decreed for the Children of Israel...').
citations: Gabriel Said Reynolds, *The Qur'an and the Bible: Text and Commentary* (Yale University Press, 2018), pp. 200–204.
Abraham Geiger, *Was hat Mohammed aus dem Judenthume aufgenommen?* (1833).
Holger Zellentin, *The Qur'an's Legal Culture: The Didascalia Apostolorum as a Point of Departure* (Mohr Siebeck, 2013).

receptionClaims.subject: The Universal vs. Particular Manuscript Tradition
receptionClaims.text: The earliest and most authoritative manuscripts of the Mishnah (including the Kaufmann Manuscript and the Jerusalem Talmud) contain the universal reading: 'whoever destroys a single soul... saves a single soul' (nefesh ahat), which matches the universal wording in Qur'an 5:32. Later Babylonian Talmud manuscripts added the qualifier 'of Israel' (mi-yisrael), reflecting a later communal application.
receptionClaims.limit: Scholarly consensus overwhelmingly favors the shorter, universal reading as original to the tannaitic Mishnah.

receptionClaims.subject: The Universal Principle of Human Sanctity
receptionClaims.text: In Islamic jurisprudence, Surah 5:32 establishes that all human life created by Allah possesses inherent inviolability (*hurmah*). Slaying any innocent person—regardless of religion or lineage—is regarded as a cosmic assault against the entire human family.

receptionClaims.limit: Exemptions apply only to lawful judicial capital punishment for murder or violent corruption (*fasad fi al-ard*).
